landing.description: // Write Java code. Watch the compiler dissect it — token by token, tree by tree, instruction by instruction.

why.label: // WHY_THIS_EXISTS
why.headline: Compilers are black boxes.
why.body: Most tools show compile success or failure. This one shows how Java becomes bytecode — lex, parse, AST, semantic analysis, bytecode generation — then runs the result.
why.compilerVsInterpreter: A compiler translates the whole program before it runs; an interpreter executes it line by line. Java is a hybrid — javac compiles to bytecode, the JVM interprets it, and a JIT compiler turns hot code into native machine code.

steps.title: FRONT END
steps.description: Understands your code: the scanner, parser, and semantic elaboration turn source text into an intermediate representation (IR).

steps.title: OPTIMIZER
steps.description: Analyzes the IR and rewrites it into better IR — same meaning, faster code. Data-flow analysis, loop-invariant code motion, and more.

steps.title: BACK END
steps.description: Maps the IR to the target machine: instruction selection, scheduling, and register allocation produce the final program.

step1.title: Regular Expressions
step1.description: Each token type is defined by a regex pattern. These patterns describe what valid tokens look like in Java.
step1.caption: How it works: each token type is a regular expression; the scanner turns those REs into machines in the next step.
step1.examplesHint: Try It — type your own RE and see its parse tree. Precedence: () > * + ? > concat > |
step1.precedenceHint: Precedence: () highest, then * + ?, then concatenation, then | lowest
step1.slashHint: — did you mean | for alternation? / is literal.
step1.recognizerHint: Each circle is a state, each arrow is labelled by the next input character. Double circles are accepting states. Missing transitions go to the error state and are omitted.
step1.recognizerTooLarge: Recognizer too large to display — try a shorter RE.

walkthrough.label: Example walkthrough — Recognizing words
walkthrough.step1Recog: RE new is three symbols concatenated n·e·w. The recognizer is a linear chain s0 —n→ s1 —e→ s2 —w→ s3. Only s3 is accepting.
walkthrough.step2Recog: RE new | not shares the prefix n. From s0 —n→ s1 the recognizer branches: s1 —e→ s2 —w→ s3 (new) versus s1 —o→ s4 —t→ s5 (not). Two accepting states.
walkthrough.step3Recog: Adding while merges the start state: s0 has n and w. The while path is s0 —w→ s6 —h→ s7 —i→ s8 —l→ s9 —e→ s10. Three accepting states s3, s5, s10.
walkthrough.step4Recog: RE a(a|0)* — an alphabetic character followed by zero or more letters or digits. Needs a cycle: s0 —a→ s1, with a loop s1 —a|0→ s1. All words like a, a0, aa0 are accepted. Same idea gives integers 0 | [1-9][0-9]*.

step2.title: Finite Automaton (NFA) — Thompson Construction
step2.description: Each regex pattern is turned into a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton — a graph of circles (states) and arrows (transitions). Built with Thompson's construction (RE → NFA). ε marks empty-string transitions.
step2.caption: How it works: each token pattern becomes a small machine with one start and one accept. The unified start fans out to all patterns via ε.
step2.overviewHint: The unified start state fans out via ε-transitions into one machine per token pattern — select a token type below to inspect how it was built.
step2.flatHint: Full combined NFA: every state and ε/symbol edge laid left→right in layers — the true combined machine.
step2.buildHint: Examples: step-by-step walkthrough for a(b|c)* — symbols → b|c → (b|c)* → a·(b|c)*. Use 1–4 to step.
step2.keywordHint: Showing {{shown}} of {{hidden}} keyword branches — the rest are collapsed behind the dashed bridge.

step3.title: DFA — Subset Construction (NFA → DFA)
step3.description: Subset construction converts the NFA into a deterministic FA. This is the first fixed point — the algorithm iterates until no new DFA states are discovered.
step3.overviewHint: Summary: how many DFA states the token NFA collapses to, with ε-closure table and first subset steps.
step3.examplesHint: Type a tiny RE (max 24 chars) and watch Subset Construction build its DFA live.

minimization.title: DFA Minimization (Hopcroft)
minimization.description: Hopcroft's algorithm refines the partition of DFA states until no group can be split — the second fixed point. Each minimal state merges an equivalence class of original states.

step4.title: Scanner (on minimized DFA)
step4.description: The minimized DFA scanner reads your source code character by character, transitioning between states via Δ. Longest-match with rollback is shown; comments use a hybrid fast-path (block comments need multi-char lookahead).

tokens.hoverHint: Hover over tokens to see details

step1.title: Context-Free Grammar & Input Tokens
step1.description: The parser consumes the token stream produced by lexical analysis and checks it against the grammar of Java. Below is the token stream from the lexer, alongside the subset of context-free grammar production rules your program exercises.
step1.noRules: No grammar rules exercised by this program
step1.tryItHint: Try It — type your own expression and watch the rightmost derivation grow, then see its parse tree. Example: a + b × c
step1.tryGrammarHint: Start symbol is Goal. Terminals are name, +, -, *, /, (, ).
step1.tryTreeHint: Each derivation step expands the rightmost nonterminal — the tree shows the same rules as nested boxes.

step2.title: Pushdown Automaton (PDA)
step2.description: A parser is a finite-state machine with a stack: the Pushdown Automaton. The controller moves between states as tokens arrive, while the stack remembers partially-parsed constructs. Watch both move as the parse proceeds.
step2.tryItHint: Try It — type your own expression and watch the leftmost top-down (LL(1)) parser predict, match, and accept. Example: a + b × c
step2.tryGrammarHint: Start symbol is Goal. ε is empty. This grammar is naturally LL(1) — no left recursion, perfect for top-down.

step3.title: Shift-Reduce Parser
step3.description: Tokens are shifted from the input buffer onto the parse stack one at a time. Whenever the top of the stack matches the right-hand side of a grammar rule, the parser reduces those symbols into the left-hand side non-terminal.
step3.tryItHint: Try It — type your own expression and watch the bottom-up parser shift tokens, find handles, and reduce to Goal. Example: a + b × c
step3.tryGrammarTitle: Example grammar — augmented with Goal′ → Goal
step3.tryGrammarHint: Bottom-up: shift tokens until the stack top holds a handle (right side of a rule), then reduce it to the left side. Builds a reverse rightmost derivation — left-to-right scan, one lookahead symbol.

step4.title: Abstract Syntax Tree Construction
step4.description: Each reduction builds a node of the Abstract Syntax Tree. Watch the tree grow from the leaves up — the final output of syntax analysis is the complete AST handed to semantic analysis.
step4.tryItHint: Try It — type your own expression and watch its abstract syntax tree grow: operators become internal nodes, names and numbers become leaves. Example: a + b × c

ast.hint: Click nodes to expand/collapse • Scroll to zoom • Drag to pan

semantic.name: Name
semantic.scopeTreeDescription: The compiler builds a hierarchical tree of scopes — each package contains classes, each class contains methods, and each method contains local blocks with their own variables.
semantic.symbolCollectionDescription: As the compiler traverses the AST, it collects every named entity (variables, parameters, methods, fields) and catalogs them in their respective scopes.
semantic.typeResolutionDescription: When you write System.out.println(), the compiler must resolve each part: System → java.lang.System, out → java.io.PrintStream, println → PrintStream.println(String). Watch this chain unfold.
semantic.typeCheckingDescription: The compiler verifies that every assignment, method call, and expression is type-safe. Incompatible types produce errors before bytecode is generated.
semantic.errorReportingDescription: The final phase collects all semantic errors — undeclared variables, type mismatches, and invalid method calls. The compiler only proceeds to code generation if this list is empty.

listing.title: Bytecode Listing
listing.description: Parsed javap output showing class structure, constant pool, and method bytecode instructions with opcode descriptions.

stackMachine.title: Stack Machine Simulation
stackMachine.description: JVM executes bytecode using an operand stack. Each instruction pushes/pops values from the stack, transforming the program state.

flow.title: Execution Flow
flow.description: Step-by-step execution showing how the JVM processes each bytecode instruction. Changes to stack and local variables are highlighted.

step0.title: TAC Generation
step0.description: Expressions are decomposed into three-address code (TAC). Each instruction has at most three operands: result = arg1 operator arg2. Color-coded by operation type. The optimizer's CFG is reused here — see Optimizer for basic blocks and flow edges.

step1.title: Dependence Graph
step1.description: Data (RAW), anti (WAR), and output (WAW) dependencies between instructions are identified. The longest latency-weighted chain is the critical path.

step2.title: List Scheduling
step2.description: Instructions are reordered into time slots to minimize pipeline stalls while respecting dependencies. A superscalar pipeline issues up to 2 instructions per cycle.

step3.title: Interference Graph
step3.description: Variables that are simultaneously live interfere — they cannot share a register. Each edge connects two interfering variables derived from liveness analysis.

step4.title: Graph Coloring
step4.description: Variables are assigned to physical registers using graph coloring. Excess variables are spilled to memory. Copies that land in the same register are eliminated.
step4.noData: Register allocation requires CFG data for liveness analysis.

interactions.title: Interactions
interactions.description: The back end's hard problems interact. Scheduling moves loads away from the arithmetic that uses them — this widens the period a value is live, raising register pressure. Register allocation, in turn, can create false dependencies that constrain scheduling: two operations sharing a register cannot be reordered, even when their values are independent. Renaming the values breaks the false dependence, at the cost of one more register.

step1.title: Basic Blocks
step1.description: The program is decomposed into basic blocks — maximal straight-line sequences with no branches except at the end. Leaders mark block entry points.

step2.title: Value Numbering
step2.description: Local Value Numbering assigns a number to each distinct value. When the same expression reappears with the same operand numbers, it is redundant and can be replaced by a copy.

step3.title: Dominator Tree
step3.description: Block A dominates block B if every path from the entry to B must go through A. The dominator tree shows these immediate domination relationships.

step4.title: SSA Form
step4.description: In Static Single Assignment form, every variable is assigned exactly once. φ-functions merge values at control-flow join points, and each definition gets a unique subscript.

pipeline.title: Compilation Pipeline
pipeline.subtitle: HOW JAVA COMPILES YOUR CODE
pipeline.description: Follow the journey from human-readable source code to native execution inside the JVM. Eight phases, each transforming your code into something the machine can run.
pipeline.completeDescription: From human-readable text, through IR and bytecode, to native execution inside the JVM — this is the magic behind "write once, run anywhere."

frontEnd.title: Front End
frontEnd.description: Phases 1-5: scanner, parser, elaboration — understand your code and record it as IR.

optimizer.title: Optimizer
optimizer.description: Phase 6: analyze the IR and rewrite it into better IR — same meaning, faster code.

backEnd.title: Back End
backEnd.description: Phase 7: instruction selection, scheduling, register allocation — map IR to the JVM.

whyStudy.title: // WHY STUDY COMPILERS?
whyStudy.body: A compiler is a microcosm of computer science: greedy algorithms (register allocation), dynamic programming (instruction selection), list scheduling (instruction scheduling), finite automata (scanning), pushdown automata (parsing), and fixed-point algorithms (data-flow analysis). Working inside one is a fast way to meet them all.

source.title: Source Code
source.subtitle: Human-Readable Instructions
source.explanation1: Everything starts with source code — the instructions you write in a programming language like Java. This is text that humans can read and understand.
source.explanation2: Think of it like a recipe written in English. The computer can't follow it directly — it needs to be translated into a language the machine understands.
source.explanation3: The compiler's job is to take this human-readable text and transform it, step by step, into instructions the JVM can execute.
source.javaConcept: In Java, source code lives in .java files. Each file contains a class definition. The compiler reads this file and begins the transformation pipeline.

lexical.title: Lexical Analysis
lexical.subtitle: Tokenization
lexical.explanation1: The lexer (lexical analyzer) reads your source code character by character and groups them into meaningful units called tokens — like breaking a sentence into individual words.
lexical.explanation2: For example, the word 'public' becomes a KEYWORD token, 'HelloWorld' becomes an IDENTIFIER token, and '"Hello, World!"' becomes a STRING_LITERAL token.
lexical.explanation3: This is like how you learned to read: first you recognize individual words before you can understand sentences. The lexer ignores whitespace and comments — they don't affect the program's meaning.
lexical.javaConcept: Java has 67 keywords (like class, public, static, void), identifiers (names you create), literals (fixed values), operators (+, -, =), and separators ({, }, ;). The lexer categorizes every piece of your code.

syntax.title: Syntax Analysis
syntax.subtitle: Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)
syntax.explanation1: The parser takes the flat list of tokens and organizes them into a tree structure called an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). This reveals the grammatical structure of your code.
syntax.explanation2: Think of it like diagramming a sentence in English class — identifying the subject, verb, object, and their relationships. The AST shows which parts of your code contain other parts.
syntax.explanation3: The tree structure makes it easy for later phases to understand the hierarchy: a class contains methods, methods contain statements, statements contain expressions. Each node knows its type, position, and children.
syntax.javaConcept: Java has strict grammar rules (defined in the Java Language Specification). The parser checks that your tokens follow these rules — for example, that every '{' has a matching '}', and that statements end with ';'. If not, you get a syntax error.

semantic.title: Semantic Analysis
semantic.subtitle: Scopes, Symbols, Type Resolution & Checking
semantic.explanation1: Semantic analysis checks whether your code actually makes sense — not just grammatically (syntax), but logically. It builds a hierarchical scope tree: package → class → method → block, tracking what's visible where.
semantic.explanation2: Within each scope, the compiler collects symbols — variables, parameters, methods, fields — and catalogs their types. Then it resolves type references: System → java.lang.System, out → java.io.PrintStream, println(String) → PrintStream.println(String).
semantic.explanation3: Finally, it type-checks every assignment, method call, and expression. This catches errors like assigning a String to an int, calling a method with wrong argument types, or using an undeclared variable. Only if all checks pass does the compiler proceed to code generation.
semantic.javaConcept: Java is statically typed — every variable must have a declared type, and types must be compatible. The symbol table tracks class names, method signatures, variable types, and scope nesting. The compiler uses a scope stack to resolve identifiers: it searches the innermost block first, then enclosing scopes, up to the package level.

ir.title: Intermediate Representation
ir.subtitle: Three-Address Code (IR)
ir.explanation1: The front end's final job is generating an Intermediate Representation (IR) — the compiler's definitive form of your code. Three-Address Code (TAC) is one classic IR: each instruction has at most three operands, two inputs and one output.
ir.explanation2: Think of it as a simplified, stripped-down version of your code — like reducing a complex math equation step by step. Complex expressions are broken into simple pieces: load this, call that, store the result here.
ir.explanation3: From this point on, the compiler never looks back at your source text — it works only on the IR. That is why the IR is so important: every later phase (optimizer, back end) reads and writes this one representation.
ir.javaConcept: In our example, the method call System.out.println('Hello, World!') gets decomposed into: load the System class, access its out field, load the string constant, then call println. Each step is one simple instruction.

bytecode.title: Bytecode
bytecode.subtitle: JVM Instructions
bytecode.explanation1: The back end maps the optimized IR onto the JVM instruction set — choosing which instruction implements each IR operation (instruction selection), in what order they run (scheduling), and which values live in registers (allocation). The final output is Java bytecode: compact instructions the JVM can execute, saved in .class files.
bytecode.explanation2: Think of bytecode as an assembled recipe — every instruction is precise, numbered, and ready to follow. The JVM reads these instructions one by one and executes them on your machine.
bytecode.explanation3: This is why Java is 'write once, run anywhere' — the same bytecode runs on any device that has a JVM, whether it's Windows, Mac, or Linux. The bytecode is platform-independent; the JVM handles the platform-specific details.
bytecode.javaConcept: The javac compiler produces .class files containing bytecode. You can examine them with javap -c (the Java class file disassembler). Each bytecode instruction is one byte long (hence the name), with opcode 0-255.

optimizer.title: Optimizer
optimizer.subtitle: Analysis & Transformation
optimizer.explanation1: Between the front end and the back end sits the optimizer: an IR-to-IR transformer. It reads IR, analyzes it, and rewrites it into IR that is smaller or faster — same meaning, better code. (An IR-to-IR transformer is itself a compiler!)
optimizer.explanation2: Every optimization is a pair: analysis discovers facts about the code, transformation uses those facts to rewrite it. Data-flow analysis, for example, reasons at compile time about how values flow when the program runs.
optimizer.explanation3: The classic example is loop-invariant code motion. If an expression inside a loop never changes, the optimizer proves it is safe to compute it once before the loop — cutting work from every iteration. Context makes all the difference.
optimizer.javaConcept: javac performs only light optimization. The heavy lifting happens in the JIT compiler at runtime, which knows things a static compiler cannot — like which methods are actually called the most (hot code).

execution.title: Execution
execution.subtitle: JVM Interpreter + JIT
execution.explanation1: A virtual machine is a simulator for some processor — an interpreter for that machine's instruction set. The compiled .class file is not run by your CPU directly — it is run by the Java Virtual Machine. The JVM loads the class, verifies the bytecode, and interprets it instruction by instruction.
execution.explanation2: Interpretation is simple and portable, but slower than native code. So the JVM watches which code runs most often: when a method gets hot, a Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler translates its bytecode into native machine code for your specific CPU.
execution.explanation3: This hybrid — compile to bytecode, interpret, then JIT-compile the hot parts — is why Java is both 'write once, run anywhere' and fast enough for servers and games.
execution.javaConcept: Your CPU never sees Java bytecode. It only executes native machine instructions produced by the JIT. Next time you see a 'warm-up' before Java benchmarks, you know why: the JIT needs a moment to find the hot code.
